doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

chapter: State of jazz and its audience
title: Healthy music, sick industry
summary: Mandel judges the music healthy and dynamic worldwide while the industry is ailing, and says jazz is like air.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Right. When you are in this environment here at this jazz convention, it’s probably unrealistic. It seems that the music is so healthy in this environment. What’s your realistic view of where it’s at?

I think the music is very healthy. I think the industry is rather sick. I think we’re in a time of great change as to how to disseminate this music and figuring out what function it serves, what’s the social utility of jazz today. But I think that — realistically I do think that jazz permeates American culture and has made significant inroads into culture, basically all around the world. I think it’s a very dynamic art form. I think it’s a very adaptive art form. I think it’s got a lot of strategies and techniques, tactics that can be © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-

applied to many — that many people who want to express themselves can apply their own cultural material and their own internal feelings through the forms that jazz offers. And I think that that’s been widely recognized. And I think that in Europe or in Asia or Australia or South America we are hearing musics that could only have been created after exposure to jazz. And I think in America, yes this festival gives us — or this convention gives us a somewhat skewered view. Here are all these people running around. But I mean I recognize you come to Toronto in January in kind of a recession that we’re experiencing economically, this is the hard core of the jazz proponents here. They do represent a larger general overall market. But whenever I travel I hear jazz on the radio, I see it on TV, you don’t see it like features, here’s an hour of a jazz artist, but you hear it in commercials, you hear it in background music, you know it’s the music of our time and of our country and I really think that it’s impossible to ignore. It’s a little bit like air, we just breathe it and we don’t necessarily think about it all the time.
